heckles.text: Eleven new repos land in a README and the commit message is "docs: scribe update", which tells me about as much as a shrug. The math at least checks out

Commit message says "docs: scribe update" and that tells me jack shit. Which docs? Updated how? Both files show up as brand new, so this isn't an update at all, it's the first time README.md and CHANGELOG.md exist, and the changelog claims the app has been around since April. Three entries of history, zero docs for six months, and now it's "scribe update." Christ. The README is named "Restaurant Design and Setup Survey" while the repo is called ghost-kitchen-builder, and the word ghost kitchen appears nowhere in it, so somebody is confused about what this thing is, and it might be the README. The "Latest change" paragraph in README.md is copy pasted word for word from the top CHANGELOG.md entry, which is a stale-doc time bomb the next time anything ships. That entry is also mush: "replaced the broken cloud connection with a simpler built in sync" doesn't say which connection, what broke, or what "built in sync" means, and the April entry about connecting to the shared restaurant data service sounds suspiciously like the same thing that later broke. "Added a new color palette" is equally useless, since it doesn't say what the palette is or why anyone should care. The README also has no run instructions, no setup, nothing for a human who wants to touch this code, but it does find room to tell me Control Troll checks the app every morning, which is a status line cluttering a project description. Credit where it's due: the README does say what the tool does in plain words (completeness meter, sample concepts, copyable export), and the changelog is at least in newest-first order. Low bar, cleared.

Well, this is a push that says "scribe update" and delivers two files of pure paperwork, so I got nothing to test, nothing to play, and not a single goddamn key to press. The commit message "docs: scribe update" tells me fuck all about what changed, and it's even a little dishonest, because the changelog says "Created the app" while the diff contains no app. Maybe the code landed in another push, maybe it's hiding under a tarp, but from here this is a brochure for a piano that may or may not exist. CHANGELOG.md is one line with a date, a version, and a sentence all mashed together with commas like a ransom note. Then README.md copies that exact same sentence word for word under "Latest change," so now you've got the same fact living in two places, and the second one goes stale the minute you ship version 2. The README also says "Computer keys also play notes" without saying which computer keys, which is like handing someone a piano and telling them it has some buttons. I'll give it this much: the description is clear about who the thing is for, the light theme is a sane choice, and the plain-language rundown of octaves, sustain, and knobs is easy to follow. Fine. Move on.

Fix it: Write a real commit message in the commit itself, naming what actually changed instead of "scribe update." Delete the "Latest change" paragraph in README.md and let the line pointing to CHANGELOG.md do its job. Break the single line in CHANGELOG.md into a clean entry with the version as a heading-style line and the notes underneath, so the next entry has somewhere to go. Add the actual computer key mapping to README.md so people know which keys play which notes. Make sure the app code is in the repo, because the changelog is bragging about something this diff does not show.

Jesus, a docs-only push with the commit message "docs: scribe update", which tells me exactly nothing about what got scribed or why. You ran a bug hunt pass and the diff contains zero bug fixes, just a changelog and a README, so either the fixes went in somewhere else or the hunt came back with its dick in its hand. CHANGELOG.md is a brand new file with one line, and README.md then points at it for "the full history" like there's a library in there instead of a single sentence. That same sentence is copy pasted into the README under "Latest change", so now you have two places to forget to update. "Moved the app to GitHub" and "Triggered a production build" aren't changes anyone using the app gives a shit about, that's you clearing your throat. The README also says nothing about how to run the damn thing, what env vars it needs, or what it pulls video data from, so anyone who clones it gets a name that is just YouTube spelled backwards and no idea what to do next. The pitch itself, small channels, thirty second samples, no repeats, is at least clear and I'll grudgingly admit it's a decent elevator line.

Fix it: Rewrite the commit message so it says what actually changed, like "docs: add README and initial changelog". Put the actual bug fixes from the hunt pass into CHANGELOG.md as real entries, one per fix, instead of the vague "after a bug hunt pass" line. Delete the "Latest change" section in README.md so the changelog is the only place that history lives. Add setup steps to README.md covering install, run, and any env vars or API keys the app needs, and say where the video data comes from. Drop "Triggered a production build" from CHANGELOG.md since a deploy is not a change.

Well, the commit messages promise a playbook, a building kit, inventory and turn tools, a run log, six example turns, a dashboard, and an API runner, and the diff I got to look at is five lines in one shell script. So I can only heckle the plumbing, and the plumbing is a goddamn raid on the neighbor's toolbox. In orange-agent-setup-v1.sh, the Anthropic key step now cd's into Blue's folders and runs railway variables against blue-agent-api to lift Blue's production key and hand it to Orange. That means two agents share one key, one bill, and one blast radius, so if Orange does something stupid with it, Blue goes down too. The whole thing is wrapped in 2>/dev/null and || true, so when the railway call fails, or you're logged out, or the service is renamed, the script just shrugs and carries on with an empty AK like nothing happened. The hardcoded $HOME/blue-agent and $HOME/blue-agent/blue-agent-backend paths are guesses about one machine's folder layout. Right below it sits the LINKS loop that already scans the Railway config for linked projects and does the same hunt, so now you've got two separate key-finding mechanisms stacked on each other like a couple of drunks holding each other up. The for loop with the continue-if-already-found check is a clumsy way to say "stop at the first hit." The grep for sk-ant at the start of the value is a decent sanity check, I'll give you that, and cut -f2- keeps any equals signs in the value intact. Also, a file called setup-v1 that gets modified in place is a v1 that keeps changing, which is not what v1 means.

Fix it: Give Orange its own Anthropic key in orange-agent-setup-v1.sh instead of pulling Blue's from blue-agent-api,
